steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on compositional verification of neural network controlled systems with inductive invariants. Explain what NNCSs are, why checking inductiveness is hard with current tools, our idea of splitting the check into two conditions via a Bridge predicate, and a short summary of the method and experimental results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- NNCSs and the difficulty of formally verifying them
- Inductive invariant method; inductiveness check as formula (1)
- Why formula (1) is infeasible for current tools
- Our compositional method: Bridge predicate, conditions (2) and (3)
- Section 3 overview and Section 4 results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural Network Controlled Systems (NNCSs) are closed-loop systems made of an environment that is controlled by a neural network (NN). Because of advancements in machine learning, NNCSs have become more widespread in safety-critical applications like autonomous cars, industrial control, and healthcare. There are many methods for formal verification of standard closed-loop systems, but the scale and nonlinearity of NNs make it challenging to apply these methods directly to NNCSs.

In this paper we study formal verification of safety properties of NNCSs, and we use the inductive invariant method. Basically, the method consists in finding a state predicate IndInv which is inductive, is an invariant, and implies safety (see Section 2, Conditions (4), (5) and (6)). The most important property, and often the hardest one to check, is inductiveness. For NNCSs, checking inductiveness means checking the validity of the following formula, where \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} and \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} are the transition relation predicates of the NN controller and of the environment, and \phi^{\prime} is the state predicate \phi applied to the next-state (primed) variables:

The problem that motivates our work is that checking formula (1) is not feasible in practice with state-of-the-art tools. Generic tools like SMT solvers cannot handle formula 1 directly, usually because of the size and complexity of the NN and the corresponding \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} predicate. Specialized NN verification tools also cannot handle formula (1) directly, usually because of limitations in dealing with closed-loop systems and the environment transition relation \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} (which might for example be non-deterministic).

- Compositional method
  - break formula (1) into two separate conditions (2) and (3)
  - Bridge: new state predicate, invented automatically
  - each smaller than (1); (2) by NN verifier, (3) by SMT solver
- Section 3
  - automatic Bridge construction, establishes Condition (2) by construction
  - heuristic to falsify inductiveness compositionally when (1) not valid
  - algorithm checking inductiveness of candidate IndInv predicates
- Section 4 results
  - consistently terminates; deterministic and non-deterministic setups; NNs up to 2\times 1024 neurons; seconds
  - monolithic method times out after one hour for NNs larger than 2\times 56 neurons

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural Network Controlled Systems (NNCSs) are closed-loop systems made of an environment that is controlled by a neural network (NN). Because of advancements in machine learning, NNCSs have become more widespread in safety-critical applications like autonomous cars, industrial control, and healthcare. There are many methods for formal verification of standard closed-loop systems, but the scale and nonlinearity of NNs make it challenging to apply these methods directly to NNCSs.

In this paper we study formal verification of safety properties of NNCSs, and we use the inductive invariant method. Basically, the method consists in finding a state predicate IndInv which is inductive, is an invariant, and implies safety (see Section 2, Conditions (4), (5) and (6)). The most important property, and often the hardest one to check, is inductiveness. For NNCSs, checking inductiveness means checking the validity of the following formula, where \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} and \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} are the transition relation predicates of the NN controller and of the environment, and \phi^{\prime} is the state predicate \phi applied to the next-state (primed) variables:

The problem that motivates our work is that checking formula (1) is not feasible in practice with state-of-the-art tools. Generic tools like SMT solvers cannot handle formula 1 directly, usually because of the size and complexity of the NN and the corresponding \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} predicate. Specialized NN verification tools also cannot handle formula (1) directly, usually because of limitations in dealing with closed-loop systems and the environment transition relation \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} (which might for example be non-deterministic).

This paper proposes a compositional method for this problem. The key idea is that instead of checking formula (1) monolithically, we break it up into two separate conditions:

where Bridge is a new state predicate that has to be invented (we propose a technique to do this automatically). Each of the formulas (2) and (3) is smaller than the monolithic formula (1), and they can also be handled by the corresponding specialized tool: formula (2) by a NN verifier, and formula (3) by an SMT solver.

We elaborate our approach in Section 3. We propose a technique for constructing Bridge predicates automatically, and we show how this technique can also establish the validity of Condition (2) by construction. We also present a heuristic which can falsify inductiveness compositionally in some cases where formula (1) is not valid. These techniques are put into an algorithm that checks inductiveness of candidate IndInv predicates for NNCSs.

Our experimental results (Section 4) show that our algorithm always terminates and effectively verifies or falsifies the inductiveness of the given candidate, in both deterministic and non-deterministic environment setups, for NNs of sizes up to 2\times 1024 neurons, in a matter of seconds. The monolithic method on the other hand times out after one hour for all our experiments with NNs larger than 2\times 56 neurons.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural Network Controlled Systems (NNCSs) are closed-loop systems consisting of an environment controlled by a neural network (NN). Advancements in machine learning have made NNCSs more widespread in safety-critical applications, such as autonomous cars, industrial control, and healthcare [1]. While many methods exist for the formal verification of standard closed-loop systems [2], the scale and nonlinearity of NNs make the direct application of these methods to NNCSs challenging.

In this paper, we study formal verification of safety properties of NNCSs using the inductive invariant method [3]. In a nutshell, the method consists in finding a state predicate IndInv which is inductive, is an invariant, and implies safety (see Section 2, Conditions (4), (5) and (6)). The most important property, and often the most difficult to check, is inductiveness. In the case of NNCSs, checking inductiveness amounts to checking the validity of the following formula, where \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} and \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} are the transition relation predicates of the NN controller and of the environment, respectively, and \phi^{\prime} is the state predicate \phi applied to the next-state (primed) variables:

The problem motivating our work is that checking formula (1) is infeasible in practice using state-of-the-art tools. On the one hand, generic tools such as SMT solvers [4] cannot handle formula 1 directly, typically due to the size and complexity of the NN and the corresponding \textit{Next}_{\textit{NNC}} predicate. On the other hand, specialized NN verification tools [5,6] cannot handle formula (1) directly either, typically due to limitations in dealing with closed-loop systems and the environment transition relation \textit{Next}_{\textit{ENV}} (which, for example, might be non-deterministic).

This paper proposes a compositional method to deal with this problem. The key idea is the following: instead of checking formula (1) monolithically, we propose to break it up into two separate conditions:

where Bridge is a new state predicate that needs to be invented (we propose a technique to do this automatically). Not only is each of the formulas (2) and (3) smaller than the monolithic formula (1), they can also be handled by the corresponding specialized tool: formula (2) by a NN verifier, and formula (3) by an SMT solver.

We elaborate our approach in Section 3. We propose a technique to construct Bridge predicates automatically, and show how this technique can also establish the validity of Condition (2) by construction. We also present a heuristic that can falsify inductiveness compositionally in some cases when formula (1) is not valid. We incorporate these techniques into an algorithm that checks inductiveness of candidate IndInv predicates for NNCSs.

Our experimental results (Section 4) indicate that our algorithm consistently terminates, effectively verifying or falsifying the inductiveness of the given candidate in both deterministic and non-deterministic environment setups, for NNs of sizes up to 2\times 1024 neurons, in a matter of seconds. In contrast, the monolithic method times out after one hour for all our experiments with NNs larger than 2\times 56 neurons.
